It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). The paper you're looking for is Chebrolu et al., "Quality of anticoagulation with warfarin in rural Chhattisgarh, India," *Indian Journal of Medical Research* 2020;152(3):303-307. It is open access and is indexed in PubMed Central (PMC7881821).

**Key findings:**
- **Design:** The authors retrospectively reviewed INR data from 2014–2016 at a secondary healthcare system in rural Chhattisgarh. The INR data were retrospectively obtained from all patients taking warfarin during 2014-2016 at a secondary healthcare system in rural Chhattisgarh, India. TTR was calculated only for patients with at least two INR visits.
- **Cohort:** The 249 patients had 2839 INR visits.
- **TTR:** The median TTR was very low, at 13.0% (IQR 0–34.8). Patients spent a median of 77.5% of time below range. The median time subtherapeutic was 77.5 per cent (45-100), and the median time supratherapeutic was 0.0 per cent (0-11.6).
- **Distance:** TTR did not track with distance to the clinic (Spearman's ρ = 0.009, P = 0.906), per the paper's table.
- **Conclusion:** The authors report that INR values were subtherapeutic two-thirds of the time, and TTR values were poor regardless of distance from the health centre. They call for studies to identify interventions that could improve INR control.

**Context:** The paper notes that in most of rural India, warfarin is the only oral anticoagulant available. A TTR of 70% or more is generally treated as the goal, since it improves outcomes.

**Source:** Zilla P, Human P, Pennel T. "Mechanical valve replacement for patients with rheumatic heart disease: the reality of INR control in Africa and beyond." *Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine*, 2024 (Perspective article, published 9 February 2024; doi:10.3389/fcvm.2024.1347838).

**1. INR results in therapeutic range (RHD, mechanical valves)**
- **Patients:** 552 consecutive mechanical valve recipients for RHD.
- **INR results:** 21,826 tests over 8 years (the abstract says ">20,000").
- **Country:** South Africa (Groote Schuur Hospital, University of Cape Town, 2015–2023).
- **Result:** "Only 27% of these test results were in the therapeutic range," with 61% sub-therapeutic. The body text and Figure 1B instead describe 27% of *time* (TTR 27.2% ± 24.1%), so the abstract's wording appears to be imprecise.

**2. TTR: LMICs vs. industrialised countries**
- **Industrialised:** Safe anticoagulation is defined as TTR >60%–70% (abstract). The body text says a meta-analysis of 38 studies found de facto TTR of 59%–67%.
- **LMICs (abstract):** TTR "in the range of twenty to forty percent."
- **LMICs (body, by country):** China 43%, Thailand 42%, South Africa 49%, Ethiopia 28%, India 44%, and under 40% in a multi-country LMIC study.

**3. India 10-year mortality (mechanical MVR, young patients)**
- 41% after mechanical MVR, and 28% after mechanical AVR.
- **Cited study:** John S, Ravikumar E, Jairaj PS, Chowdhury U, Krishnaswami S (1990), "Valve replacement in the young patient with rheumatic heart disease. Review of a twenty-year experience," *J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg* (reference 18).

**4. Point-of-care INR / self-management in LMICs**
- The article does not discuss point-of-care INR testing or self-management in LMICs in any depth.
- The only relevant statement is in the Discussion: "nor are sophisticated self-tests for controlling anticoagulation available," which is a claim about valve companies' context.
- The authors also note that patients were educated by social workers before discharge on the importance of ongoing INR tests.

- **Treatment rates:** In a multinational rheumatic heart disease cohort with patients from India, only 4.4% underwent valve surgery. That is a study-population figure, not a national one.
- **Valve type:** Patients receive mechanical valves. The population is younger than in high-income countries and the disease is different, mostly of rheumatic origin. Another source says Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is one of the common indications for heart-valve surgery in India.
- **Mechanical valve use:** Mechanical valves are favored partly because the limited affordability of repeated surgeries in low- and middle-income nations like India have further boosted their usage.

The paper you're looking for is Chebrolu et al., "Quality of anticoagulation with warfarin in rural Chhattisgarh, India," *Indian Journal of Medical Research* 2020;152(3):303-307. It is open access and is indexed in PubMed Central (PMC7881821).

**Key findings:**
- **Design:** The authors retrospectively reviewed INR data from 2014–2016 at a secondary healthcare system in rural Chhattisgarh. The INR data were retrospectively obtained from all patients taking warfarin during 2014-2016 at a secondary healthcare system in rural Chhattisgarh, India. TTR was calculated only for patients with at least two INR visits.
- **Cohort:** The 249 patients had 2839 INR visits.
- **TTR:** The median TTR was very low, at 13.0% (IQR 0–34.8). Patients spent a median of 77.5% of time below range. The median time subtherapeutic was 77.5 per cent (45-100), and the median time supratherapeutic was 0.0 per cent (0-11.6).
- **Distance:** TTR did not track with distance to the clinic (Spearman's ρ = 0.009, P = 0.906), per the paper's table.
- **Conclusion:** The authors report that INR values were subtherapeutic two-thirds of the time, and TTR values were poor regardless of distance from the health centre. They call for studies to identify interventions that could improve INR control.

**Context:** The paper notes that in most of rural India, warfarin is the only oral anticoagulant available. A TTR of 70% or more is generally treated as the goal, since it improves outcomes.

=== 36036525 Rivaroxaban in Rheumatic Heart Disease-Associated Atrial Fibrillation. | The New England journal of medicine 2022

Background

Testing of factor Xa inhibitors for the prevention of cardiovascular events in patients with rheumatic heart disease-associated atrial fibrillation has been limited.

Methods

We enrolled patients with atrial fibrillation and echocardiographically documented rheumatic heart disease who had any of the following: a CHA2DS2VASc score of at least 2 (on a scale from 0 to 9, with higher scores indicating a higher risk of stroke), a mitral-valve area of no more than 2 cm2, left atrial spontaneous echo contrast, or left atrial thrombus. Patients were randomly assigned to receive standard doses of rivaroxaban or dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonist. The primary efficacy outcome was a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, or death from vascular (cardiac or noncardiac) or unknown causes. We hypothesized that rivaroxaban therapy would be noninferior to vitamin K antagonist therapy. The primary safety outcome was major bleeding according to the International Society of Thrombosis and Hemostasis.

Results

Of 4565 enrolled patients, 4531 were included in the final analysis. The mean age of the patients was 50.5 years, and 72.3% were women. Permanent discontinuation of trial medication was more common with rivaroxaban than with vitamin K antagonist therapy at all visits. In the intention-to-treat analysis, 560 patients in the rivaroxaban group and 446 in the vitamin K antagonist group had a primary-outcome event. Survival curves were nonproportional. The restricted mean survival time was 1599 days in the rivaroxaban group and 1675 days in the vitamin K antagonist group (difference, -76 days; 95% confidence interval [CI], -121 to -31; P<0.001). A higher incidence of death occurred in the rivaroxaban group than in the vitamin K antagonist group (restricted mean survival time, 1608 days vs. 1680 days; difference, -72 days; 95% CI, -117 to -28). No significant between-group difference in the rate of major bleeding was noted.

Conclusions

Among patients with rheumatic heart disease-associated atrial fibrillation, vitamin K antagonist therapy led to a lower rate of a composite of cardiovascular events or death than rivaroxaban therapy, without a higher rate of bleeding. (Funded by Bayer; INVICTUS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02832544.). === 27378324 Self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulation. | The Cochrane database of systematic reviews 2016

Background

The introduction of point-of-care devices for the management of patients on oral anticoagulation allows self-testing by the patient at home. Patients who self-test can either adjust their medication according to a pre-determined dose-INR (international normalized ratio) schedule (self-management), or they can call a clinic to be told the appropriate dose adjustment (self-monitoring). Increasing evidence suggests self-testing of oral anticoagulant therapy is equal to or better than standard monitoring. This is an updated version of the original review published in 2010.

Objectives

To evaluate the effects on thrombotic events, major haemorrhages, and all-cause mortality of self-monitoring or self-management of oral anticoagulant therapy compared to standard monitoring.

Search methods

For this review update, we re-ran the searches of the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), 2015, Issue 6, the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE (Ovid, 1946 to June week 4 2015), Embase (Ovid, 1980 to 2015 week 27) on 1 July 2015. We checked bibliographies and contacted manufacturers and authors of relevant studies. We did not apply any language restrictions .

Selection criteria

Outcomes analysed were thromboembolic events, mortality, major haemorrhage, minor haemorrhage, tests in therapeutic range, frequency of testing, and feasibility of self-monitoring and self-management.

Data collection and analysis

Review authors independently extracted data and we used a fixed-effect model with the Mantzel-Haenzel method to calculate the pooled risk ratio (RR) and Peto's method to verify the results for uncommon outcomes. We examined heterogeneity amongst studies with the Chi(2) and I(2) statistics and used GRADE methodology to assess the quality of evidence.

Main results

We identified 28 randomised trials including 8950 participants (newly incorporated in this update: 10 trials including 4227 participants). The overall quality of the evidence was generally low to moderate. Pooled estimates showed a reduction in thromboembolic events (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.75; participants = 7594; studies = 18; moderate quality of evidence). Both, trials of self-management or self-monitoring showed reductions in thromboembolic events (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.70; participants = 3497; studies = 11) and (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.97; participants = 4097; studies = 7), respectively; the quality of evidence for both interventions was moderate. No reduction in all-cause mortality was found (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.01; participants = 6358; studies = 11; moderate quality of evidence). While self-management caused a reduction in all-cause mortality (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.84; participants = 3058; studies = 8); self-monitoring did not (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.15; participants = 3300; studies = 3); the quality of evidence for both interventions was moderate. In 20 trials (8018 participants) self-monitoring or self-management d === 32558968 The Table of Standard Atomic Weights-An exercise in consensus. | Rapid communications in mass spectrometry : RCM 2022 The present Table of Standard Atomic Weights (TSAW) of the elements is perhaps one of the most familiar data sets in science. Unlike most parameters in physical science whose values and uncertainties are evaluated using the "Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement" (GUM), the majority of standard atomic-weight values and their uncertainties are consensus values, not GUM-evaluated values. The Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) regularly evaluates the literature for new isotopic-abundance measurements that can lead to revised standard atomic-weight values, Ar °(E) for element E. The Commission strives to provide utmost clarity in products it disseminates, namely the TSAW and the Table of Isotopic Compositions of the Elements (TICE). In 2016, the Commission recognized that a guideline recommending the expression of uncertainty listed in parentheses following the standard atomic-weight value, for example, Ar °(Se) = 78.971(8), did not agree with the GUM, which suggests that this parenthetic notation be reserved to express standard uncertainty, not the expanded uncertainty used in the TSAW and TICE. In 2017, to eliminate this noncompliance with the GUM, a new format was adopted in which the uncertainty value is specified by the "±" symbol, for example, Ar °(Se) = 78.971 ± 0.008. To clarify the definition of uncertainty, a new footnote has been added to the TSAW. This footnote emphasizes that an atomic-weight uncertainty is a consensus (decisional) uncertainty. Not only has the Commission shielded users of the TSAW and TICE from unreliable measurements that appear in the literature as a result of unduly small uncertainties, but the aim of IUPAC has been fulfilled by which any scientist, taking any natural sample from commerce or research, can expect the sample atomic weight to lie within Ar °(E) ± its uncertainty almost all of the time. ## 32579813 Hydroxyurea Dose Escalation for Sickle Cell Anemia in Sub-Saharan Africa. | The New England journal of medicine 2020

Background

Hydroxyurea has proven safety, feasibility, and efficacy in children with sickle cell anemia in sub-Saharan Africa, with studies showing a reduced incidence of vaso-occlusive events and reduced mortality. Dosing standards remain undetermined, however, and whether escalation to the maximum tolerated dose confers clinical benefits that outweigh treatment-related toxic effects is unknown.

Methods

In a randomized, double-blind trial, we compared hydroxyurea at a fixed dose (approximately 20 mg per kilogram of body weight per day) with dose escalation (approximately 30 mg per kilogram per day). The primary outcome was a hemoglobin level of 9.0 g or more per deciliter or a fetal hemoglobin level of 20% or more after 24 months. Secondary outcomes included the incidences of malaria, vaso-occlusive crises, and serious adverse events.

Results

Children received hydroxyurea at a fixed dose (94 children; mean [±SD] age, 4.6±1.0 years) or with dose escalation (93 children; mean age, 4.8±0.9 years); the mean doses were 19.2±1.8 mg per kilogram per day and 29.5±3.6 mg per kilogram per day, respectively. The data and safety monitoring board halted the trial when the numbers of clinical events were significantly lower among children receiving escalated dosing than among those receiving a fixed dose. At trial closure, 86% of the children in the dose-escalation group had reached the primary-outcome thresholds, as compared with 37% of the children in the fixed-dose group (P<0.001). Children in the dose-escalation group had fewer sickle cell-related adverse events (incidence rate ratio, 0.43; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.34 to 0.54), vaso-occlusive pain crises (incidence rate ratio, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.56), cases of acute chest syndrome or pneumonia (incidence rate ratio, 0.27; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.56), transfusions (incidence rate ratio, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.43), and hospitalizations (incidence rate ratio, 0.21; 95% CI, 0.13 to 0.34). Laboratory-confirmed dose-limiting toxic effects were similar in the two groups, and there were no cases of severe neutropenia or thrombocytopenia.

Conclusions

Among children with sickle cell anemia in sub-Saharan Africa, hydroxyurea with dose escalation had superior clinical efficacy to that of fixed-dose hydroxyurea, with equivalent safety. (Funded by the Doris Duke Charitable Foundation and the Cincinnati Children's Research Foundation; NOHARM MTD ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03128515.).

Here's what the search turned up. Nothing shows a finished, commercially available, low-cost CBC device for rural India that reports neutrophil counts from a finger prick.

- **IIT Kharagpur spinning-disc kit:** Researchers there have developed a spinning disc-based device that can perform Complete Blood Count (CBC) test with 95 per cent accuracy at a claimed cost of about Rs 10. Per the institute, the kit is a simple low-cost motorized spinning disc-based design. Its stated use is rural healthcare, and the sources don't say whether it reports neutrophils specifically. The kit is still described as a proof of concept in the paper and press coverage.
- **Adsys Medtech (Jaipur):** A government technology listing describes a device to generate a point of care CBC report in minutes - with a fingerprick. Its status is listed as proof of concept, and the listing doesn't give cost or neutrophil performance.
- **IISc microfluidic chip:** A Nature Scientific Reports paper describes a low-cost portable microfluidic chip based device for the widely used 14 parameter complete blood count (CBC). This is a research prototype and the snippets don't give its price.
- **LeukoScope (not Indian):** This is the closest match on neutrophils and finger-prick sampling. It is a low-cost system to measure a WBC and neutrophil count from a single drop of blood at the point of care. Clinical testing used fingerprick samples collected from 105 general oncology patients in Houston, TX, and it correctly identified five out of six patients with abnormal neutrophil counts, versus six of six for HemoCue WBC DIFF. It is a WBC/neutrophil device, not a full CBC.

Caveats: the Rs 10 figure and 95% accuracy come from institute and press statements, not an independent peer-reviewed validation in the results. The results also contain little on regulatory approval or field trials in India.

The search turned up one Indian national document, though I couldn't confirm its exact date or that it was issued by NHM.

- **Dosing (ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow, sickle cell disease):** The advisory document gives infants and children 10-15 mg/kg/day and adolescents 15 mg/kg/day. It allows escalation in 5 mg/kg steps, and only for definite indications. The same document's flowchart is also on the ICMR site, and it states that CBC should be checked 1-3 months after starting the drug or after any dose change. The file is hosted on ICMR's site (STW series) rather than the NHM site, and the search didn't show a "2023" date. Check the PDF's front matter before citing it.
- **Context:** A 2025 systematic review notes that India approved 500 mg HU capsules for sickle cell anaemia in December 2021, after the drug had been used off-label. A review by ICMR researchers reports that low-dose HU (10 mg/kg/day) reduced vaso-occlusive crisis rates, hospitalization, and transfusion need.
- **Conflicting international guidance:** The 2014 US expert panel recommends a higher starting dose for children, 20 mg/kg/day, with CBC monitoring at least every 4 weeks during dose adjustment. It also allows escalation to a maximum of 35 mg/kg/day.
- **Open question:** An Indian randomized trial comparing 10 vs 20 mg/kg/day is ongoing. Its authors state that the effectiveness of low-dose HU compared to the standard dose remains uncertain.

Bottom line: the Indian national workflow supports low-dose starting (10-15 mg/kg/day) with CBC checks at 1-3 month intervals, while the 2014 US panel uses a higher starting dose with more frequent monitoring. I did not find a separate NHM 2023 hydroxyurea protocol in these results.

**Sickle cell figures from the Health Dialogues article (published 2 Aug 2025)**

- **Screened:** 6,04,50,683 (about 6.05 crore) people, as of 28 July 2025. The article says screening covered 17 tribal-dominated states.
- **Diagnosed with sickle cell disease:** 2,16,118.
- **Carriers:** More than 16.7 lakh (1.67 million+). The article notes carriers may not show symptoms but can pass the gene to their children.
- **Source:** Union Health Minister JP Nadda, answering a question in the Lok Sabha on "Friday." The article gives no Rajya Sabha answer. The publication date suggests Friday was 1 August 2025, but the article doesn't state the exact date.
- **State ranking (cases registered on the national sickle cell portal):**
  1. Odisha: 96,484
  2. Madhya Pradesh: 30,580
  3. Gujarat: 28,150
  4. Chhattisgarh: 26,104
  5. Maharashtra: 23,218
  - Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, and Jharkhand also reported "notable" numbers, but no figures are given. Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Uttarakhand, and Himachal Pradesh are described as having "far fewer cases," with no figures.
- **Hydroxyurea:** Added to the National Health Mission's list of essential medicines. The article states it "is now available even at sub-health centres."
- **Patients on hydroxyurea or in follow-up:** No figures provided.
- **Related figure:** More than 2.62 crore genetic counselling ID cards have been distributed. These categorise individuals as normal, carrier, or affected.
- **Target:** Screen 7 crore people aged 0–40 in tribal areas by the end of FY 2025–26.

I didn't find an Indian Academy of Neurology workforce study from 2024, and no source gives a reliable current count. The estimates I found vary widely:

- **Lowest figure:** A Hindustan Times piece (reprinted on PressReader, 2021) puts the total at fewer than 2,500 neurologists in India with 1.4 billion people.
- **Mid-range:** An SEO-style explainer gives approximately 2,500-3,500 qualified neurologists, while another gives around 6,000 – 7,000 neurologists. Neither cites a primary source, so I'd treat them as weak.
- **Modelled rate:** A STRIDE dementia desk review modelled about 4.3 neurologists for every 100,000 populations, heavily concentrated in main cities. That figure is a model, not a census.
- **Association membership:** A 2015 count found 3,812 neurologists were associated with the professional associations for neurologists in India, which is about approximately 70% of the total, implying a total near 5,400. This is the only source I found that ties the count to a professional body.

On official data, a February 2023 Lok Sabha answer said that the data regarding the total number of neurological patients and the present ratio of neurologist to neurological patients in the country is not maintained centrally. On training, one source says the number of specialist training positions in neurology has increased from 30 in 1990 to 500 in 2020. A July 2026 Biospectrum report says the country's neurologist-to-patient ratio is nearly 80 times worse than that of high-income countries, but I couldn't access the report itself to check its figures.

The sources agree that neurologists are concentrated in cities. For a defensible number, search directly for the Indian Academy of Neurology's own publications or the Neurology India journal, since the 2015 Ganapathy analysis is the most cited basis.

## 39024737 10.1016/j.bcmd.2024.102873 Sickle cell disease in Indian tribal population: Findings of a multi-centre Indian SCD registry. | Blood cells, molecules & diseases 2024

Background

Sickle cell disease (SCD) registries provide crucial real-world data on demographics, epidemiology, healthcare, patient outcomes, and treatment efficacy. This paper presents findings from the Indian SCD Registry (ISCDR) on clinical manifestations, crisis episodes, disease management, and healthcare utilization in patients with SCD from 12 primary health centres (PHCs) in six tribal districts of India.

Methods

The ISCDR was introduced along with a three-tier screening process. Its Android-based application incorporates two electronic case report forms for patient data collection over one year. This paper presents a year's data from the ISCDR's 324 patients with SCD.

Results

Patients with SCD, aged one to 65 years, exhibited varied clinical manifestations. Most patients (85.2 %) were unaware of their SCD status before enrolling in ISCDR. Moderate to severe anaemia was prevalent (66.05 % and 30.56 %, respectively). Pain was a common complaint (80.86 %; CI: 76.17-85.00), while symptoms of stroke included sudden severe headaches (34.57 %; CI: 29.40-40.02). Common splenic sequestration symptoms included stomach pain (42.90 %; CI: 37.44-48.49) and abdominal tenderness (13.27 %; CI: 9.77-17.46), as a sign. Healthcare utilization was high, with 96.30 % receiving treatment and 83.64 % consuming hydroxyurea. Hospitalization occurred for 38.27 % (CI: 32.95-43.81), and 12.04 % (CI: 8.70-16.09) had blood transfusion during last year.

Conclusions

ISCDR serves as a dynamic digital database on SCD epidemiology, clinical aspects, treatment and healthcare utilization. Notably, many patients lacked prior awareness of their SCD status, underscoring the need for improved awareness and care management. Integrating the registry into the national programme can streamline treatment implementation, prioritize management approaches, and optimize individual benefits. ## 36213959 10.1002/epi4.12659 A cluster-randomized trial comparing home-based primary health care and usual clinic care for epilepsy in a resource-limited country. | Epilepsia open 2022

Objective

To ascertain whether home-based care with community and primary healthcare workers' support improves adherence to antiseizure medications, seizure control, and quality of life over routine clinic-based care in community samples of people with epilepsy in a resource-poor country.

Methods

Participants included consenting individuals with active epilepsy identified in a population survey in impoverished communities. The intervention included antiseizure medication provision, adherence reinforcement and epilepsy self- and stigma management guidance provided by a primary health care-equivalent worker. We compared the intervention group to a routine clinic-based care group in a cluster-randomized trial lasting 24 months. The primary outcome was antiseizure medication adherence, appraised from monthly pill counts. Seizure outcomes were assessed by monthly seizure aggregates and time to first seizure and impact by the Personal Impact of Epilepsy scale.

Results

Enrolment began on September 25, 2017 and was complete by July 24, 2018. Twenty-four clusters, each comprising ten people with epilepsy, were randomized to either home- or clinic-care. Home-care recipients were more likely to have used up their monthly-dispensed epilepsy medicine stock (regression coefficient: 0.585; 95% confidence intervals, 0.289-0.881; P = 0.001) and had fewer seizures (regression coefficient: -2.060; 95%CI, -3.335 to -0.785; P = 0.002). More people from clinic-care (n = 44; 37%) than home-care (n = 23; 19%) exited the trial (P = 0.003). The time to first seizure, adverse effects and the personal impact of epilepsy were similar in the two arms.

Significance

Home care for epilepsy compared to clinic care in resource-limited communities improves medication adherence and seizure outcomes and reduces the secondary epilepsy treatment gap.

**Title:**
"Comparative Analysis of Hematological Parameters in Indian Sickle Cell Anemia Patients" "Treated with Low Dose (10mg/kg/day) Versus Standard Dose (20mg/kg/day) Hydroxyurea"

**Authors/Institutions:**
Naveen Khargekar (presenting author), Manisha Madkaikar, Neha Kargutkar, Anindita Banerjee, and Namrata Mahajan are affiliated with the ICMR-National Institute of Immunohaematology in Mumbai, India. Kalpna Gupta is affiliated with the Hematology/Oncology Division, Department of Medicine, University of California, Irvine.

**Why low dose is used:**
The abstract says Indian physicians often prescribe the low dose, and it gives this reason: "Low dose is recommended by most of the physicians in India due to fear of adverse events." It adds that concern about patients not returning for regular blood monitoring also plays a role.

**Trial design:**
The study is described as a national-level randomized controlled trial of children with sickle cell anemia. Patients were randomized to ARM 1 (10 mg/kg/day hydroxyurea) or ARM 2 (20 mg/kg/day). The abstract notes that the trial was still in progress when it was submitted.

**Number of patients:**
- 140 patients (ages 2–14) were enrolled after informed consent.
- 37 completed 6 months of follow-up: 18 in ARM 1 (mean age 8.9 ± 2.8 years) and 19 in ARM 2 (mean age 8.6 ± 2.5 years).
- Clinical severity: 26 patients were class I and 10 were class II.

**HbF and other results (6 months):**
- **HbF:** The rise was greater in ARM 2 (4.81 ± 2.71%) than in ARM 1 (1.55 ± 2.32%).
- **WBC:** Decreased more in ARM 2 (4.08 ± 2.6 ×10³/µl) than in ARM 1 (2.18 ± 2.24 ×10³/µl).
- **Platelets:** Decreased more in ARM 2 (50 ± 127.39 ×10³/µl) than in ARM 1 (24 ± 136.6 ×10³/µl).
- **Hemoglobin:** Rose by 0.18 ± 0.71 g/dL in ARM 1 and 0.71 ± 0.77 g/dL in ARM 2.
- **MCV:** Rose by 3.29 ± 2.61 fL in ARM 1 and 5.28 ± 3.57 fL in ARM 2. The abstract reports P<0.001 for both arms.
- **RBC:** No significant increase in either arm.
- **ANC:** Reported as reduced in ARM 2, with the abstract giving 2874 ± 1748 per µL versus 1963 ± 1748 per µL in ARM 1. The identical standard deviations are worth verifying against the full data.
- **Safety:** Two ARM 2 patients had ANC below 1000 per µL. Their hydroxyurea was stopped and restarted after one week.
- **Severity and baseline HbF:** 6 of 10 patients (60%) with baseline HbF below 15% had class II severity, compared with 3 (11.5%) of those with HbF above 15%.
- **Clinical events:** No vaso-occlusive crises, strokes, or acute chest syndrome were recorded at baseline or at 6 months.

**Conclusion:**
The authors state that hydroxyurea "led to a significant increase in HbF levels in ARM II" compared with ARM I. They report that WBC, platelet, and ANC levels were lower in ARM 2, which they say calls for close monitoring. They also note the absence of critical clinical events over 6 months, suggesting benefit in both arms, and call for longer follow-up to confirm these findings.

# D5-01 High-stakes conditions: which serious disease to build the loop for (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-16)

Why this note exists: the user asked to replace the blood-pressure pick with a serious, specific disease. Here a missed or wrong dose does real harm within days or weeks, a specialist normally makes the dose decisions, and rural patients see that specialist rarely. This note compares four candidates on the same rubric as `DT1-triage.md`, adds a "harm per missed or wrong dose" column, and records the facts behind each score.

Fact IDs are D5-01-Fxx. OPENED means the source page or abstract was read; SNIPPET means only a search summary was seen. Heart-failure facts reuse the existing D1-01 IDs.

## Digest

Answer: build the loop for **warfarin in rheumatic heart disease**, meaning patients with a mechanical valve or with AF caused by a rheumatic valve. Keep **sickle cell hydroxyurea dosing** as the second protocol on the same engine. Under the old rubric the two are level (3.70 and 3.75). Once harm per missed or wrong dose is weighted, warfarin leads (4.03 and 3.56). OUR ARITHMETIC

Facts that matter most:
1. In rural India, INR control is far worse than the rest of the world, and it fails on the low side. At a rural Chhattisgarh hospital the median time in range was 13.0%, and patients spent a median 77.5% of time below range and 0% above. Distance to the clinic did not explain it. (D5-01-F03) The gap is in how doses are set, not in how far patients travel, and setting doses is what the loop does.
2. India holds 13.2 million of the world's 33 million people with rheumatic heart disease (RHD), 40%, and about 120,000 of 347,000 RHD deaths (2015). (D5-01-F01) This corrects the plan's "about a third", which is the share of deaths, not of patients.
3. RHD patients on warfarin cannot switch to newer blood thinners. In INVICTUS (4,531 patients, mean age 50.5, 72.3% women), rivaroxaban led to more events and more deaths than warfarin-type drugs, with no difference in major bleeding. (D5-01-F04)
4. The loop itself has survival proof. When patients tested INR at home and set the dose from a fixed schedule, deaths fell (RR 0.55) and clots fell (RR 0.47). When they tested at home and phoned the clinic, deaths did not fall (RR 0.94). (D5-01-F05)
5. Sickle cell: national screening found 2,16,118 patients by 28 July 2025, and hydroxyurea is stocked down to sub-health centres. (D5-01-F12) India's own workflow keeps the dose at 10-15 mg/kg and raises it only "in definite indications", with a blood count 1-3 months after each change. (D5-01-F13) Raising the dose to about 30 mg/kg cut sickle events (IRR 0.43) and hospital stays (IRR 0.21) in Ugandan children, with the same toxicity. (D5-01-F14) Indian doctors keep doses low out of "fear of adverse events and noncompliance of patients for regular monitoring of blood parameters". (D5-01-F15)
6. Epilepsy drops to third. No trial was found in which non-specialists adjust the dose. The one Indian trial tested home delivery of medicine and adherence support, not dose changes. (D5-01-F21, F22)

Surprises:
- Under-dosing, not over-dosing, is the main warfarin failure in rural India (D5-01-F03). A loop that steps the dose up safely has more room to help than one that only guards against bleeding.

- How many Indians take warfarin for RHD.
- The Indian price of a CoaguChek meter.
- An Indian startup running remote INR or hydroxyurea dosing; none was found in one search each.

The last two columns differ in one way. "Old rubric" is the DT1 weighting. "Harm lens" gives harm per missed or wrong dose a weight of 25 and scales the other six weights to three quarters (0.75 x old + 0.25 x harm). All scores are OUR VIEW.

| Condition and loop | Proof | Market | Feasibility | Gap | Deep-tech | Low risk | Harm per dose | Old rubric | Harm lens | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Warfarin in RHD (mechanical valve, rheumatic AF): INR reading, then dose | 5 | 3 | 3 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 3.70 | 4.03 | D5-01-F01, F03, F04, F05, F09; OUR VIEW |

| Heart failure: weight, BP, pulse, then diuretic and drug steps | 4 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 3.30 | 3.48 | D1-01-F27, F31, F47; OUR VIEW |
| Epilepsy: seizure count, then drug steps | 2 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 3.20 | 3.40 | D5-01-F19 to F22; OUR VIEW |
| Reference: blood-pressure step loop (DT1 scores, overnight feasibility) | 5 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 4.35 | 3.76 | DT1-triage.md; OUR VIEW |

Reasons, one line each (OUR VIEW):
- **Warfarin.**
  - Proof 5: the Cochrane mortality signal comes from exactly this loop (F05).
  - Gap 5: rural time in range is 13% and no Indian service was found (F03, F11).
  - Harm 5: a valve clot or a bleed can follow within weeks, in either direction.
  - Market 3: 13.2 million people have RHD (F01), but the number on warfarin is unknown, and non-valve AF can move to newer drugs (F03).
  - Feasibility 3: strips cost about Rs 649 each (F09), so the likely model is a shared meter at the health centre or ASHA level, not one meter per patient.
  - Low risk 2: a wrong dose can kill, so every change needs a clinician's tap and the INR targets must be hard limits.
- **Sickle cell.**
  - Market 4: 2.16 lakh diagnosed patients, the government already pays, and hydroxyurea is free (F12).
  - Proof 4: the trial was in children in Uganda and was not a digital loop (F14).
  - Feasibility 3: no cheap finger-prick blood count is on sale (F17).
  - Harm 3: a missed dose costs benefit over weeks, not days.
  - The main risk is that the loop would push doses above the national workflow (F13).
- **Heart failure.** Unchanged from DT1 except that feasibility rises to 3 for a pilot with health-centre lab tests. Many Indian heart-failure patients have RHD, so it can share the warfarin pilot's patients.
- **Epilepsy.** Proof 2: no dose-loop trial was found, and the Indian trial tested medicine supply and adherence (F21, F22). The rural need is real (F19).
- **Blood pressure.** It still scores highest on the old rubric, which rewarded overnight buildability and patient pool size. On the user's harm lens it falls behind warfarin.

## What changes for the build (OUR VIEW)

- The engine stays as it is (D2-01). The protocol file changes:
  - INR reading in place of the BP reading.
  - A warfarin dose schedule keyed to the target range: 2.0-3.0, or 2.5-3.5 for mechanical mitral valves (D5-01-F03).
  - The "was the medicine taken" check comes before any step-up, because 77.5% of time below range may partly reflect missed tablets rather than too low a dose (F03).
- The measurement becomes a health-centre or ASHA-held INR meter. A home meter per patient is not affordable at about Rs 649 a strip (F09). OUR ESTIMATE
- The pilot measures time in range at 3 months against the clinic's own baseline, which F03 puts near 13%. This shows a result far faster than blood pressure could.
- Sickle cell is the second protocol in the same file format: dose per kg, a blood-count gate before each step, a hold rule on low neutrophils, and pain days as the symptom input. Pitch it as the government-payer expansion.

## Open items for a next pass

- Count of Indians on warfarin for RHD: try REMEDY India and CSI, or hospital anticoagulation clinic volumes (SCTIMST, CMC Vellore, AIIMS).
- Indian CoaguChek meter price, and Indian-made INR meters.
- Competitors searched by name: hospital anticoagulation clinics, and diagnostics chains offering home INR collection.
- The Lok Sabha primary PDF for F12.
- India's 2023 sickle cell mission guideline, if it updates the 2020 workflow dose.

Why this note exists: the user asked to replace the blood-pressure pick with a serious, specific disease. Here a missed or wrong dose does real harm within days or weeks, a specialist normally makes the dose decisions, and rural patients see that specialist rarely. This note compares four candidates on the same rubric as `DT1-triage.md`, adds a "harm per missed or wrong dose" column, and records the facts behind each score.

Fact IDs are D5-01-Fxx. OPENED means the source page or abstract was read; SNIPPET means only a search summary was seen. Heart-failure facts reuse the existing D1-01 IDs.

Answer: build the loop for **warfarin in rheumatic heart disease**, meaning patients with a mechanical valve or with AF caused by a rheumatic valve. Keep **sickle cell hydroxyurea dosing** as the second protocol on the same engine. Under the old rubric the two are level (3.70 and 3.75). Once harm per missed or wrong dose is weighted, warfarin leads (4.03 and 3.56). OUR ARITHMETIC

Facts that matter most:
1. In rural India, INR control is far worse than the rest of the world, and it fails on the low side. At a rural Chhattisgarh hospital the median time in range was 13.0%, and patients spent a median 77.5% of time below range and 0% above. Distance to the clinic did not explain it. (D5-01-F03) The gap is in how doses are set, not in how far patients travel, and setting doses is what the loop does.
2. India holds 13.2 million of the world's 33 million people with rheumatic heart disease (RHD), 40%, and about 120,000 of 347,000 RHD deaths (2015). (D5-01-F01) This corrects the plan's "about a third", which is the share of deaths, not of patients.
3. RHD patients on warfarin cannot switch to newer blood thinners. In INVICTUS (4,531 patients, mean age 50.5, 72.3% women), rivaroxaban led to more events and more deaths than warfarin-type drugs, with no difference in major bleeding. (D5-01-F04)

5. Sickle cell: national screening found 2,16,118 patients by 28 July 2025, and hydroxyurea is stocked down to sub-health centres. (D5-01-F12) India's own workflow keeps the dose at 10-15 mg/kg and raises it only "in definite indications", with a blood count 1-3 months after each change. 6. Epilepsy drops to third. No trial was found in which non-specialists adjust the dose. The one Indian trial tested home delivery of medicine and adherence support, not dose changes. (D5-01-F21, F22)

- Under-dosing, not over-dosing, is the main warfarin failure in rural India (D5-01-F03). A loop that steps the dose up safely has more room to help than one that only guards against bleeding.

- How many Indians take warfarin for RHD.

Here a missed or wrong dose does real harm within days or weeks, a specialist normally makes the dose decisions, and rural patients see that specialist rarely. Fact IDs are D5-01-Fxx. OPENED means the source page or abstract was read; SNIPPET means only a search summary was seen. Heart-failure facts reuse the existing D1-01 IDs.

Keep **sickle cell hydroxyurea dosing** as the second protocol on the same engine. Under the old rubric the two are level (3.70 and 3.75). Facts that matter most:
1. In rural India, INR control is far worse than the rest of the world, and it fails on the low side. At a rural Chhattisgarh hospital the median time in range was 13.0%, and patients spent a median 77.5% of time below range and 0% above. Distance to the clinic did not explain it. (D5-01-F03) The gap is in how doses are set, not in how far patients travel, and setting doses is what the loop does.
2. India holds 13.2 million of the world's 33 million people with rheumatic heart disease (RHD), 40%, and about 120,000 of 347,000 RHD deaths (2015). (D5-01-F01) This corrects the plan's "about a third", which is the share of deaths, not of patients.
3. RHD patients on warfarin cannot switch to newer blood thinners. In INVICTUS (4,531 patients, mean age 50.5, 72.3% women), rivaroxaban led to more events and more deaths than warfarin-type drugs, with no difference in major bleeding. (D5-01-F04)
4. The loop itself has survival proof. When patients tested INR at home and set the dose from a fixed schedule, deaths fell (RR 0.55) and clots fell (RR 0.47). When they tested at home and phoned the clinic, deaths did not fall (RR 0.94). (D5-01-F05)
5. Sickle cell: national screening found 2,16,118 patients by 28 July 2025, and hydroxyurea is stocked down to sub-health centres. (D5-01-F12) India's own workflow keeps the dose at 10-15 mg/kg and raises it only "in definite indications", with a blood count 1-3 months after each change. (D5-01-F13) Raising the dose to about 30 mg/kg cut sickle events (IRR 0.43) and hospital stays (IRR 0.21) in Ugandan children, with the same toxicity. 6. Epilepsy drops to third. No trial was found in which non-specialists adjust the dose. The one Indian trial tested home delivery of medicine and adherence support, not dose changes. (D5-01-F21, F22)

- Under-dosing, not over-dosing, is the main warfarin failure in rural India (D5-01-F03). A loop that steps the dose up safely has more room to help than one that only guards against bleeding.

  - https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36213959/ (2022). OPENED (abstract via Europe PMC).
- D5-01-F22. BRIDGE (Nigeria): cluster-randomised non-inferiority trial. Community health workers prescribe and adjust four anti-seizure drugs by a standard protocol, supervised by a physician. Outcome: share of children seizure-free for more than 6 months at 24 months. No results were found. https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/75/NCT04290975/Prot_000.pdf (protocol). SNIPPET.

### Heart failure (existing IDs, not re-researched)

- STRONG-HF, rapid up-titration: readmission or death RR 0.66 (D1-01-F27).
- TIM-HF2: the benefit grew with distance from a cardiologist (D1-01-F31).
- India's national registry: 47.5% of eligible patients received guideline drugs; mortality 14.2% at 90 days and 22.1% at 1 year (D1-01-F47, F48).

## Scores

Weights as in `DT1-triage.md`: proof 25, market 20, feasibility 20, gap 15, deep-tech 10, low risk 10. Feasibility now means "a 6-month pilot" rather than "built overnight", because the event is over.

The last two columns differ in one way. "Old rubric" is the DT1 weighting. "Harm lens" gives harm per missed or wrong dose a weight of 25 and scales the other six weights to three quarters (0.75 x old + 0.25 x harm). All scores are OUR VIEW.

| Condition and loop | Proof | Market | Feasibility | Gap | Deep-tech | Low risk | Harm per dose | Old rubric | Harm lens | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Warfarin in RHD (mechanical valve, rheumatic AF): INR reading, then dose | 5 | 3 | 3 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 3.70 | 4.03 | D5-01-F01, F03, F04, F05, F09; OUR VIEW |
| Sickle cell: hydroxyurea raised by blood count and weight | 4 | 4 | 3 | 5 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3.75 | 3.56 | D5-01-F12 to F17; OUR VIEW |
| Heart failure: weight, BP, pulse, then diuretic and drug steps | 4 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 3.30 | 3.48 | D1-01-F27, F31, F47; OUR VIEW |
| Epilepsy: seizure count, then drug steps | 2 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 3.20 | 3.40 | D5-01-F19 to F22; OUR VIEW |
| Reference: blood-pressure step loop (DT1 scores, overnight feasibility) | 5 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 4.35 | 3.76 | DT1-triage.md; OUR VIEW |

Reasons, one line each (OUR VIEW):
- **Warfarin.**
  - Proof 5: the Cochrane mortality signal comes from exactly this loop (F05).
  - Gap 5: rural time in range is 13% and no Indian service was found (F03, F11).
  - Harm 5: a valve clot or a bleed can follow within weeks, in either direction.
  - Market 3: 13.2 million people have RHD (F01), but the number on warfarin is unknown, and non-valve AF can move to newer drugs (F03).
  - Feasibility 3: strips cost about Rs 649 each (F09), so the likely model is a shared meter at the health centre or ASHA level, not one meter per patient.
  - Low risk 2: a wrong dose can kill, so every change needs a clinician's tap and the INR targets must be hard limits.
- **Sickle cell.**
  - Market 4: 2.16 lakh diagnosed patients, the government already pays, and hydroxyurea is free (F12).
  - Proof 4: the trial was in children in Uganda and was not a digital loop (F14).
  - Feasibility 3: no cheap finger-prick blood count is on sale (F17).
  - Harm 3: a missed dose costs benefit over weeks, not days.
  - The main risk is that the loop would push doses above the national workflow (F13).
- **Heart failure.** Unchanged from DT1 except that feasibility rises to 3 for a pilot with health-centre lab tests. Many Indian heart-failure patients have RHD, so it can share the warfarin pilot's patients.
- **Epilepsy.** Proof 2: no dose-loop trial was found, and the Indian trial tested medicine supply and adherence (F21, F22). The rural need is real (F19).
- **Blood pressure.** It still scores highest on the old rubric, which rewarded overnight buildability and patient pool size. On the user's harm lens it falls behind warfarin.

## What changes for the build (OUR VIEW)

- The engine stays as it is (D2-01). The protocol file changes:
  - INR reading in place of the BP reading.
  - A warfarin dose schedule keyed to the target range: 2.0-3.0, or 2.5-3.5 for mechanical mitral valves (D5-01-F03).
  - The "was the medicine taken" check comes before any step-up, because 77.5% of time below range may partly reflect missed tablets rather than too low a dose (F03).
- The measurement becomes a health-centre or ASHA-held INR meter. A home meter per patient is not affordable at about Rs 649 a strip (F09). OUR ESTIMATE
- The pilot measures time in range at 3 months against the clinic's own baseline, which F03 puts near 13%. This shows a result far faster than blood pressure could.
- Sickle cell is the second protocol in the same file format: dose per kg, a blood-count gate before each step, a hold rule on low neutrophils, and pain days as the symptom input. Pitch it as the government-payer expansion.

## Open items for a next pass

- Count of Indians on warfarin for RHD: try REMEDY India and CSI, or hospital anticoagulation clinic volumes (SCTIMST, CMC Vellore, AIIMS).
- Indian CoaguChek meter price, and Indian-made INR meters.
- Competitors searched by name: hospital anticoagulation clinics, and diagnostics chains offering home INR collection.
- The Lok Sabha primary PDF for F12.
- India's 2023 sickle cell mission guideline, if it updates the 2020 workflow dose.

I wrote the note, and it still points to **warfarin for rheumatic heart disease** (people with a mechanical valve, or with AF caused by a rheumatic valve). Sickle cell is a close second. It's in [D5-01 High-stakes conditions.md](research_notes/dtx/D5-01%20High-stakes%20conditions.md). It has 22 facts, most opened at the source, and it passes `check_report.py`. Every fact links through `link_facts.py`.

**What the research added:**
- **The rural problem is under-dosing, not distance.** A rural Chhattisgarh hospital (249 patients) kept patients in the safe INR range only 13% of the time, and below range 77.5% of the time. Distance to the clinic made no difference. The failure is in how doses are set, which is what a dose loop fixes.
- **Correction to what I told you earlier:** India has 40% of the world's rheumatic heart disease patients (13.2 million of 33 million, 2015 figures). "About a third" is India's share of the deaths.
- **These patients have to stay on warfarin.** I re-opened the INVICTUS trial abstract (4,531 patients): rivaroxaban led to more deaths than warfarin-type drugs, with no less bleeding.
- **The survival proof holds.** Re-checked at the source: patients who tested INR at home and dosed from a schedule died less often (RR 0.55). Those who phoned the clinic instead did not (RR 0.94).
- **The market is narrower than "everyone on warfarin".** In the Chhattisgarh group only 10% had a mechanical valve, and 84% could have used a newer blood thinner if they could afford it. The patients who truly can't switch are those with valves or rheumatic AF.
- **Sickle cell carries a guideline risk.** India's 2020 treatment workflow caps hydroxyurea at 10–15 mg/kg and raises it only "in definite indications". A Uganda trial (NOHARM-MTD) found raising it to about 30 mg/kg cut hospital stays sharply (IRR 0.21) with the same side effects. So the loop would be asking doctors to go above the national guidance, a risk the warfarin loop doesn't carry.
- **Epilepsy drops to last.** I found no trial in which non-specialists adjust the dose; the one Indian trial tested home delivery of medicine and adherence support.

**Scores** (old weights; then with harm from a missed or wrong dose given a weight of 25):

| Condition | Old score | With harm weighted |
|---|---|---|
| Warfarin, rheumatic heart disease | 3.70 | **4.03** |
| Sickle cell, hydroxyurea | 3.75 | 3.56 |
| Heart failure | 3.30 | 3.48 |
| Epilepsy | 3.20 | 3.40 |

On the old weights blood pressure still scores 4.35, mostly because it was buildable overnight, but with harm weighted it falls to 3.76, behind warfarin.

**For the build:** the engine stays as it is; only the protocol file changes. A test strip costs about ₹649, so the realistic setup is one INR meter shared at the health centre or by the ASHA worker, not one per patient. The pilot would measure time in the safe range at 3 months, starting from a baseline near 13%.

**Still unknown:** how many Indians take warfarin for rheumatic heart disease, and what a CoaguChek meter costs in India. I also couldn't download the Lok Sabha source for the sickle cell screening numbers, so they come from a news report of that answer.

I added the new pick to your TechSparks project memory. Nothing is committed.
